name: Cannabis / CBD for sleep
summary: Cannabis and cannabidiol are used for sleep onset, but clinical evidence is limited and CBD supplements are not FDA-approved for sleep.
lead: Cannabis and cannabidiol (CBD) are used by some people to help with sleep onset. The only FDA-approved CBD medicine, Epidiolex (2018), is indicated for certain seizure disorders, not sleep .

name: Alcohol as sleep aid
summary: Using alcohol to fall asleep is common; reference sources describe drowsiness alongside disrupted sleep architecture, and facial effects are mainly a looksmaxxing claim.
lead: Using alcohol as a sleep aid means drinking in the evening to fall asleep faster. Wikipedia reports that alcohol can cause drowsiness while disrupting sleep architecture, particularly later REM sleep, and that it lowers sleep quality and can greatly worsen existing sleep problems .

name: Trazodone / prescription sleep meds
summary: A prescription antidepressant widely used off-label for sleep; evidence for insomnia is modest and there are no appearance studies.
lead: Trazodone is a prescription antidepressant of the serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor class. It was developed by Angelini Research Laboratories in Italy in the 1960s, marketed in Italy from 1972, and approved by the US FDA in 1981 . Its labelled use is major depressive disorder, but at lower doses it is widely prescribed off-label for insomnia .

name: Zolpidem (Ambien)
summary: A prescription Z-drug sleeping pill with a boxed warning for complex sleep behaviors; no appearance research exists.
lead: Zolpidem is a nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic, or Z-drug, sold under brand names including Ambien. It was first used in Europe in 1988 by Synthelabo, approved in the US in 1992, and became available as a generic in 2007 . It is indicated for short-term treatment of insomnia, typically two to six weeks .

name: DSIP (delta sleep-inducing peptide)
summary: A nine-amino-acid research peptide first reported in the 1970s to promote sleep; human evidence is small and old.
lead: Delta sleep-inducing peptide (DSIP), also called emideltide, is a neuropeptide with the amino acid sequence WAGGDASGE. It was reported by a Swiss group in the 1970s, who isolated it from the cerebral venous blood of sleeping rabbits .

name: Growth hormone peptides at bedtime
summary: Using GH-releasing peptides such as ipamorelin and CJC-1295 before sleep to boost the night-time GH pulse; no studies test this practice.
lead: Growth hormone peptides at bedtime refers to the practice of using growth hormone secretagogues, such as ipamorelin and CJC-1295, shortly before sleep. The stated aim is to amplify the pulse of growth hormone that occurs during sleep.

name: Morning sunlight viewing
summary: Spending time outdoors soon after waking to anchor the body clock; related to established light-therapy research, with no appearance studies.
lead: Morning sunlight viewing is a lifestyle practice in which people spend roughly ten to thirty minutes outside soon after waking, with the stated aim of anchoring the circadian clock.

name: Blue light blocking glasses
summary: Amber or tinted glasses worn in the evening to reduce blue light and protect melatonin; small trials exist, reviews of eye-health claims are mixed.
lead: Blue light blocking glasses are eyewear designed to filter part of the blue spectrum, typically 400 to 500 nm, from screens, LED lighting and sunlight. Lenses use amber or yellow dye-based tints or interference coatings, and are available with or without prescription .

name: Red light at night
summary: Swapping white evening lights for red ones to protect melatonin; the idea is plausible from light science but untested for this use.
lead: Using red or dim red bulbs instead of white light in the evening is a lighting habit in sleep-focused communities, based on the idea that long-wavelength light disturbs melatonin and the body clock less than white or blue light.

name: Screen curfew / dopamine detox
summary: Cutting screens before bed and taking breaks from stimulation; the light-and-sleep logic has support, the "dopamine" framing is disputed.
lead: A screen curfew means stopping phone, computer and TV use some time before bed, and "dopamine detox" or "dopamine fasting" is a related practice of temporarily abstaining from stimulating activities. In looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities both are discussed as ways to improve sleep and focus.

name: Consistent sleep schedule
summary: Same bed and wake times daily; a standard sleep-hygiene habit, with no trials for looks or height claims.
lead: A consistent sleep schedule means going to bed and waking at about the same times every day, including weekends. It is a standard element of sleep-hygiene advice and is discussed in looksmaxxing forums as a free way to support hormones, growth and recovery.
claims: A fixed 8.5-10 hour bedtime boosts growth hormone and testosterone, including up to 15 percent larger GH pulses.

name: Bedroom temperature (cold room, 65F)
summary: Sleeping in a cool room; recommended in sleep-hygiene advice, but the specific 65 F figure is untested here.
lead: The cold-room habit keeps the bedroom cool, often around 65 F (about 18 C), on the belief that cooler air supports sleep. It is a common item in sleep routines in looksmaxxing and wellness communities.

name: Cooling mattress pad (Eight Sleep)
summary: An app-connected bed cover that heats and cools; praised for temperature control, subscription-dependent, no looks trials.
lead: Eight Sleep is an American company founded in 2014 that sells temperature-controlled bedding, notably the Pod smart mattress cover, which actively heats or cools the bed. It is discussed in sleep-optimization communities as a way to hold a cool sleeping surface.

name: Weighted blanket
summary: A heavy blanket for calming pressure at bedtime; trial evidence exists mainly in clinical groups and is mixed.
lead: A weighted blanket is a blanket filled with pellets, glass beads or chains so that it presses evenly on the body, commonly weighing about 5 to 30 pounds (2.3 to 13.6 kg). It is used in occupational therapy for deep pressure stimulation and is sold to consumers as a sleep and anxiety aid. In sleep-focused communities it is discussed as a way to feel calmer at bedtime.

name: Sleep tracker (Oura / Whoop / Eight Sleep)
summary: Rings, bands and bed covers that score your sleep, useful as a trend log, shaky on stage accuracy.
lead: Consumer sleep trackers are wearable or bed-based devices that estimate sleep duration, sleep stages and related measures such as heart rate variability (HRV) and resting heart rate. Well-known examples include the Oura smart ring, the Whoop strap and the Eight Sleep smart mattress cover. Looksmaxxing communities discuss them as tools for monitoring sleep, which proponents link to skin, facial puffiness and energy.
claims: Tracking sleep stages and HRV helps improve sleep and, in turn, appearance
Sleep scores are accurate enough to guide decisions
Trackers can make sleep worse through fixation

name: Sleep hygiene basics
summary: Dark, cool, quiet, regular sleep habits; a sensible baseline, but weak evidence as a stand-alone insomnia fix.
lead: Sleep hygiene is a set of behavioral and environmental practices intended to promote healthy sleep, such as a regular schedule and a dark, cool, quiet bedroom. The concept was developed in the late 1970s to help people with mild to moderate insomnia.
claims: A dark, cool, quiet, regular sleep routine improves looks
Sleep hygiene alone fixes sleep problems

name: CBT-I
summary: The guideline-recommended first-line therapy for chronic insomnia; nothing tested on looks directly.
lead: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, multi-component treatment for chronic insomnia that combines techniques such as stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive therapy, relaxation and sleep hygiene. It is described as the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia.
claims: CBT-I is the gold-standard fix for insomnia
Fixing insomnia with CBT-I improves appearance

name: Caffeine cutoff (no caffeine after noon)
summary: Stop caffeine by noon to protect sleep; plausible given half-life, but the exact cutoff is untested.
lead: The caffeine cutoff is a habit of stopping caffeine intake by a set time, often noon or early afternoon, to protect sleep. Proponents say better sleep benefits skin and appearance.
claims: No caffeine after noon improves sleep and looks

name: Late-night eating cutoff
summary: Stop eating about 3h before bed for less puffiness and better sleep; untested in this form.
lead: The late-night eating cutoff is the practice of stopping food about three hours before bed. Proponents say it reduces morning facial puffiness and improves sleep.
claims: Stopping eating 3 hours before bed reduces puffiness and improves sleep

name: Evening hot shower / bath
summary: A warm shower or bath before bed for faster sleep onset; thinly sourced here.
lead: The evening hot shower or bath is a pre-bed routine that proponents say promotes sleep onset by relaxing the body and, as it cools afterward, lowering core temperature.
claims: A hot shower or bath before bed helps you fall asleep faster

name: Sauna
summary: Heat bathing with a strong cardiovascular research base in Finnish cohorts, and no studies at all on the facial and bone claims made online.
lead: A sauna is a small room heated to high temperatures, typically 70-105 C with low humidity, where people sit to sweat, often with bursts of steam made by pouring water on hot stones.  The practice is most associated with Finland, whose sauna culture UNESCO listed as intangible cultural heritage in 2020.  Variants include smoke, electric, steam and infrared saunas.
claims: Sauna raises growth hormone and aids gains.
Regular sauna use increases brow-ridge bone mass and attractiveness.
Sauna is important for health and longevity.

name: Magnesium oil / Epsom salt bath
summary: Soaking in magnesium sulfate or applying magnesium chloride brine, popular for transdermal magnesium claims that have little published trial support.
lead: Epsom salt is the common name for magnesium sulfate heptahydrate, named after a saline spring in Epsom, Surrey, England.  It is used externally as bath salts, especially foot soaks to soothe sore feet.  Magnesium oil, despite its name, is typically a magnesium chloride brine sprayed on skin; it is a separate product.

name: Grounding / earthing mat
summary: Conductive sheets and mats meant to connect the sleeper to the earth, with no strong published evidence for sleep or appearance benefits in the sources reviewed.
lead: Grounding or earthing refers to an alternative medicine practice in which people make direct contact with the earth, or with conductive products connected to it, in the belief that this improves health.  Grounding mats and sheets are sold for sleep and plug into a socket's ground port.

name: Mouth breathing correction / myofunctional therapy
summary: Tongue, lip and nasal-breathing exercises promoted to improve breathing and facial structure, with the facial claims resting mostly on conceptual models.
lead: Mouth breathing correction describes efforts to shift breathing from the mouth to the nose, including exercises of the tongue and lips known as myofunctional therapy and, in some communities, taping the lips shut during sleep.

name: CPAP (sleep apnea)
summary: The standard treatment for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea; appearance benefits like less puffiness are discussed online but untested in the sources reviewed.
lead: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) delivers pressurised air through a mask to keep the airway open during sleep.  It was developed in adults by Colin Sullivan, who built a machine in 1980 at Royal Prince Alfred Hospital in Sydney, and Respironics began selling a commercial adult device in 1985.

name: Sleep apnea surgery / MMA
summary: Maxillomandibular advancement moves both jaws forward to open the airway, described as among the most effective sleep surgeries and often discussed for facial change.
lead: Maxillomandibular advancement (MMA), also called bimaxillary advancement or orthognathic surgery, moves the upper and lower jaws forward.  It was first used to correct facial skeletal deformities and malocclusion, and from the late 1970s advancing the lower jaw was noted to improve sleepiness in patients.

name: Face tape / sleep patches for wrinkles
summary: Overnight forehead and brow stickers promising to smooth lines in your sleep, with marketing behind them and no trial data.
lead: Face tape and sleep patches are adhesive strips or silicone and hydrocolloid-style pads that people stick on the forehead, between the brows, around the eyes or on the mouth area before bed, with the aim of flattening or preventing lines that form from facial expression or sleeping position. They are sold as cosmetic products and are not medical devices with a recognised wrinkle indication.

name: Overnight skin repair routine (retinol at night)
summary: Retinol at bedtime with a moisturiser; retinoids have real wrinkle evidence, but the 'overnight' framing itself hasn't been tested.
lead: An overnight skin repair routine is a practice of applying retinol, often alongside a moisturiser or barrier-supporting product, in the evening so that the skin is treated while the person sleeps. It is common in skincare communities and appearance-focused circles as a way to address fine lines, texture and sun damage.

name: Overnight lip/eye masks
summary: Thick balms and gels left on overnight for lips and eyes; plain moisturiser logic, no trials of the masks themselves.
lead: Overnight lip and eye masks are leave-on products, usually a thick balm, gel or sheet, applied before bed and left on while sleeping. They are marketed to moisturise the lips and the thin skin around the eyes and to soften the look of dryness and fine lines by morning.

name: Polyphasic sleep
summary: Splitting sleep into naps to sleep far less; historically interesting, and expert panels report adverse impacts.
lead: Polyphasic sleep is the practice of dividing sleep into several separate periods across 24 hours, usually more than two, rather than one consolidated nighttime block. The term was used in the early twentieth century by psychologist J. S. Szymanski to describe animal activity patterns. In online communities it refers to schedules, such as Uberman and Everyman, that aim to cut total sleep to a few hours using short naps.
claims: Short naps can replace most nighttime sleep and free up hours.
Pre-industrial humans naturally slept in segments, so polyphasic sleep is natural.
